summary.text: The Crusades were a series of military campaigns launched by the papacy between 1095 and 1291 against Muslim rulers, for the recovery and defence of the Holy Land.
The First Crusade was proclaimed by Pope Urban II at the Council of Clermont in November 1095, calling Christians to reconquer Jerusalem with promises of spiritual reward.
Its successes led to four Crusader states in the Levant, whose defence required further expeditions from Catholic Europe.

items.prompt: In 1095 a pope called Christians to arms to reconquer Jerusalem. What did he offer those who took up the call?

options.label: A share of captured cities
Spiritual reward
Freedom from all taxes at home
A noble title in the Holy Land

items.explain: The call to arms came with promises of spiritual reward, and crusade indulgences were among the institutions that large campaigns relied on.

items.prompt: A crusade sets out aiming at Egypt but ends up attacking the capital of a Christian empire. What had happened to it?

options.label: It was diverted to the Byzantine Empire and sacked Constantinople
Its ships were blown off course by storms
Its leaders changed targets after Egypt agreed to terms
It was recalled by the pope to defend Edessa

items.explain: Initially directed against Egypt, the Fourth Crusade was diverted to the Byzantine Empire, culminating in the Sack of Constantinople.

items.prompt: The Second Crusade failed in 1148, after the fall of Edessa. What effect did that failure have on crusading?

options.label: Support rose sharply, and many new Crusader states appeared
Support fell, but only in the Holy Land, not in Europe
Support fell across Latin Christendom, weakening the Crusader states
Support held steady, and Saladin was soon driven back

items.explain: The failure reduced support for crusading across Latin Christendom, leaving the Crusader states unable to resist Saladin's expansion.

items.prompt: By the 13th century, people could earn crusade indulgences through the Iberian, Albigensian and Northern campaigns. How did that affect expeditions to the eastern Mediterranean?

options.label: Enthusiasm for them diminished
Enthusiasm for them grew
They were banned by the papacy
They became far larger

items.explain: Because indulgences could also be obtained through other campaigns, enthusiasm for expeditions in the eastern Mediterranean diminished.

items.prompt: In the late 13th century a power that had reunited Egypt and Muslim Syria swept away the Crusaders' last mainland strongholds. Who was it?

options.label: The Seljuks
The Byzantines
Saladin's army
The Mamluks

items.explain: Having reunited Egypt and Muslim Syria by 1260, the Mamluks captured the Crusaders' last mainland strongholds in 1291.

items.prompt: A historian calls a papally authorised war in Iberia a crusade, though it was not fought in the Holy Land. Is that usage unusual?

options.label: Yes, because crusade only ever meant a journey to the Holy Land
No, scholars often apply the term to other papally authorised conflicts
Yes, because the papacy forbade wars outside the Holy Land
Yes, because only popular movements were called crusades

items.explain: In scholarly usage, crusade is frequently applied more broadly to papally authorised conflicts in other regions, including the Iberian Crusades.

pack.title: Why the crusades kept going
pack.question: How did one papal call in 1095 lead to nearly two centuries of campaigns?

paragraphs.heading: What the Crusades were
paragraphs.text: The Crusades were a run of wars that the popes launched between 1095 and 1291 against Muslim rulers, to win back and then hold the Holy Land. Western Christians fought them with the promise of spiritual reward. Alongside the official campaigns came unofficial ones fuelled by popular zeal, usually called popular crusades. Historians often stretch the word further, to papally approved wars elsewhere, such as the Iberian, Northern and Albigensian Crusades.

paragraphs.heading: The long road to 1095
paragraphs.text: In Roman Palestine, places tied to the ministry of Jesus became popular with pilgrims, and Christian emperors built churches there, including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. The eastern half of the Roman Empire, the Byzantine Empire, lost wide lands in the 7th century to the rising Islamic Caliphate, and Jerusalem fell to Caliph Umar in 638. By the middle of the 10th century the Muslim world had itself split into three rival caliphates.

paragraphs.heading: Clermont and the first success
paragraphs.text: In November 1095, at the Council of Clermont, Pope Urban II called on Christians to take Jerusalem back from the Muslims. The First Crusade that followed succeeded and created four Crusader states in the Levant. They were the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the counties of Edessa and Tripoli, and the Principality of Antioch. Defending them meant sending more armies from Catholic Europe. Running such huge campaigns needed complex institutions, among them crusade indulgences, the military orders and taxes on the income of the clergy.

paragraphs.heading: Setbacks and Saladin
paragraphs.text: The fall of Edessa set off the Second Crusade, which failed in 1148 and cooled enthusiasm across Latin Christendom. Saladin then joined Egypt and Muslim Syria under his rule and crushed the Crusader armies at the Battle of Hattin in 1187. The Third Crusade kept the Crusader states alive, but Jerusalem stayed in Muslim hands. The Fourth Crusade was meant for Egypt yet turned on the Byzantine Empire, sacking Constantinople in 1204.

paragraphs.heading: The last campaigns
paragraphs.text: Jerusalem was won back by negotiation in 1229, during the Sixth Crusade, but a sack of the city by Muslim freebooters soon ended Crusader rule there. King Louis IX of France led two campaigns, against Egypt in 1248–51 and against Tunis in 1270, and both failed. The Mamluks, who had reunited Egypt and Muslim Syria by 1260, then attacked the Crusader states. In 1291 they took the Crusaders' last strongholds on the mainland.

paragraphs.heading: Where the word comes from
paragraphs.text: Early writers used words for travel, such as iter, expeditio and passagium, usually naming the destination too. Those who went sewed a cross onto their clothes and were called crucesignati, "those signed with the cross". Everyday language followed this habit of taking the cross: the earliest known form, crozada, shows up in Spain in 1212. The modern word crusade was settled by 1706.
